gap: No result ChatGPT got states that 2000 W travel converters are not one circuit: on Ceptics' dual-outlet units the 2000 W hair-dryer outlet works only with dryers controlled by a mechanical button or knob, not digital or auto-shutoff dryers such as Dyson or Shark FlexStyle; the separate 200 W 'Dual Voltage' outlet on the LX2-M2000 does not convert voltage at all; and the compact 200 W PU-200X does not change 50 Hz to 60 Hz.
standout_why: I compared against globalplugs.com (says transformer-based converters are 'usually more reliable for heating appliances' but has nothing on waveform, frequency, dual-wattage outlets or digital dryers), voltwander.com/faq ('only with a high-wattage step-down converter (2000W+ to handle the dryer)', with no warning about digital or Dyson dryers and nothing on outlets that pass voltage through unconverted), and doace.com adapter-vs-converter-vs-transformer (says 'some converters output a stepped or modified waveform' and that frequency matters for clocks, fans and motors, but names no product, no outlet that skips conversion and no digital-dryer exclusion). ChatGPT's answer only said compact converters 'cannot safely handle' hair dryers. None of them tells the shopper that the 2000 W outlet ChatGPT's advice implies they need still won't run a modern digital dryer, or that one outlet on a 'converter' may deliver the full 220–240 V.
decides: If the shopper's US device is a phone, laptop or other 100–240 V electronics, a plain universal adapter is enough, and a 200–250 W converter (TESSAN TC03, Ceptics PU-200X) is for small single-voltage 110 V items only. If it is a hair dryer, the only kind of compact converter that fits is a dual-outlet 2000 W unit (Ceptics LX-C2000 or LX2-M2000), and only for dryers with a mechanical switch. A Dyson, Shark FlexStyle or any dryer with a circuit board needs Ceptics' own pure-sine VC-S2000 ($129.99; Ceptics says to plug nothing else in while a Dyson is running) or a dual-voltage dryer. Only 120 V items go on a converted outlet. The LX2-M2000's 200 W outlet passes wall voltage through, so it is safe only for devices labelled 100–240 V. A timer or clock that relies on 60 Hz needs a frequency-converting unit such as Ceptics PU-300-WS, which is out of stock.
